A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text and Appendices A–C. Theorems, proofs, equations, and presentation elements can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical inequalities, constructive sharpness examples, and theoretical estimation guarantees. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical results.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its additional proof steps and discussion do not introduce experiments, simulations, or data-analysis results.

M1.justification: The Gaussian model, Yatracos estimator, and regularized empirical Bayes procedure remain unchanged. Remark 4.9 mentions Lepskii adaptation for unknown contamination but does not specify a revised procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version uses empirical datasets or evaluation tasks. Sub-Gaussian mixing distributions are mentioned in v2 only as future work, not as newly studied data coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated baseline comparisons. Discussions of NPMLE and other estimators provide theoretical context; the new citations do not introduce experimental comparators.

E3.justification: No experimental evaluation protocols appear in either version. The theoretical observation models and loss functions are retained.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or case studies. The sharpness construction and analysis of constant dependence are retained; the added mathematical derivations concern proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing theoretical concentration bounds remain unchanged.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries in either version. The principal mathematical bounds and sharpness findings retain their constants, including 2+δ and 0.33, and their asymptotic rates.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a derivative and concavity argument establishing the subadditivity used in Theorem 4.5, which v1 merely asserts, and an explicit squared-risk step. Proposition A.3 also gains the missing square in its Cauchy–Schwarz display. These refine existing proofs without changing the principal theorem statements or assumptions.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain unchanged: sharp distance inequalities, resolution of the comparability question, entropic characterization, and robust estimation applications. The introduction's replacement of Ω by Θ summarizes behavior already claimed and supported by v1's upper and lower bounds.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the Yatracos estimator's computational inefficiency and adds G-modeling and unknown-contamination interpretations in Remarks 4.8–4.9. Section 5 adds discussion of broader mixing-distribution tails and emphasizes that optimal sample-size dependence remains open even in the clean one-dimensional case.

D1.justification: Appendix C retains the same estimator definitions, covering-radius choice, and regularization parameter formula. No implementation instructions, hardware information, or code/data access resources are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds Efron (2014), Lepskii (1991, 1992), and Polyanskiy and Wu (2021) for G-modeling, adaptive tuning, and unresolved sample-size rates. The principal positioning relative to Jia et al. (2023) is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 polishes prose throughout the introduction, applications, and proof explanations, expands several explanatory passages, and distinguishes intermediate sharpness distributions using superscript (0). These are local refinements; the organization of Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–C is retained.

P2.justification: Section 3 adds an unnumbered diagram tracing the existing construction through Lemma 3.2, Corollaries 3.3–3.4, and Theorem 3.1. Equation formatting and page flow also change locally, while the overall layout remains the same.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the existing theory easier to verify through the expanded Theorem 4.5 proof and clearer proof displays. The construction diagram, disambiguated notation, and explicit computational and applicability limitations also improve readability and interpretation. These are useful but limited gains; the central theoretical contribution remains unchanged.
